However, he observes the market has been consistently selling the stock down over the past year and believes the company needs to deliver strong profit, revenue and margin numbers to reverse the trend. He argues that if capital continues to be eroded, the 10% dividend yield becomes meaningless, and there are better places to allocate capital.
quote: I think, yeah, it is a bit of an old world business publishing, those kinds of things. They are doing some strict cost controls. So I think that that is what's going to move this. But you can tell that the market, I mean, over that 5-year chart, you sort of say, okay, well, it has done quite well. But you can see over the last sort of, over the last year that the market has been selling this down. I think they need to come out with some really good numbers on that profit revenue margin and all those kinds of things, which will then turn the stock around. So for me, it's a sell. I don't think you need to be there. 10% dividend yield, sure. But if your capital is getting eroded while that's happening, that 10% dividend yield won't last for long.

headline: Dawes (Shaw and Partners) rates REA Group a hold amid perfect storm of headwinds, flagging CGT changes and falling auction clearance rates as key risks
reasoning: Dawes acknowledges REA's dominant and lucrative position but views the company as facing a perfect storm of headwinds including competitive pressure from Domain's new US-backed partnership, ChatGPT disruption fears, and two major broker downgrades from UBS and Citi. He notes Sydney auction clearance rates have fallen to around 45-50% versus the normal ~80% for the same time of year, indicating a softening housing market. UBS cut its listing volume forecast by 10% for this year and next, and reduced its price target by 23% to $165. He sees a conditional buy case: if the proposed CGT changes do not proceed, listing volumes could rebound sharply, making REA an 'absolute screamer of a buy', but given too many unknowns he rates it a hold for now.
quote: I am a little cautious about area. As far as that. We have seen auction's rates started to fall. We're here in Sydney. I think they're around about sort of 50, 45%. Normally they're around about 80% for sort of the same time in, in, you know, in the year. So it does show that the market is changing. Now obviously if these CGT changes don't go through, which might seems like it might not. But if that doesn't happen, then Aria is an absolute screamer of a buyer, because that turnaround on those listing volumes will increase. But everybody still needs to sell. In the short term, we might see a lot of investors unloading some of their properties as well. Again, you need to be with RA for that as well. So look, for me it's a neutral. I'm going to say hold I there's too many unknowns in there. I still do have some clients in it. So we're going to sort of sit there and see how this thing goes. But if some of those do, some of those CGT changes do happen, I think this might be a really good buy, but for me it would be a hold at the moment.

headline: Australia faces a $4.7 trillion intergenerational wealth transfer driven by baby boomers and superannuation maturation, creating major complexity for advisers and families
reasoning: Chris Smith argues the intergenerational wealth transfer is not hype but a genuine structural shift, with superannuation — introduced in the early 1990s — now reaching its first transfer generation. Approximately $4.7 trillion is expected to change hands over the next 10–20 years. The transfer is more complex than previous generations' primarily property-based wealth, now encompassing superannuation, family trusts, and multi-layered structures. He notes that families and advisers are struggling to initiate these conversations due to emotional difficulty and structural complexity. Delayed conversations risk decisions being made under pressure, with surviving spouses sometimes unaware of asset locations or structures. Advisers play a critical role in navigating tax, legal, and legacy considerations for both givers and recipients.
quote: There's something like $4.7 trillion that's going to get handed over across the generations in the next little while. So, yeah, no, it's definitely real. It's not just the family home anymore. There's certainly superannuation. There's family trust. There's a lot more complexity to how assets are coming from those high net worths into the next generation. So that's adding complexity and challenges to what we see.

headline: Sean Partners' Philip Pepe sees Hello World's 20% earnings downgrade as unsurprising and structurally unimpressed by the low-moat travel agent business
reasoning: Pepe noted Hello World's downgrade was widely expected, consistent with trading updates from Qantas and Webjet. He highlighted the company suffered $170 million in cancellations and rebookings due to global conflict disruption. More fundamentally, he views travel agents as low-moat businesses with many competitors and historically low return on equity both before and after COVID. He does not expect Hello World to be a wealth-creating stock long term.
quote: These have never been businesses with great notes. There've always been so many travel agents. If you didn't like that one, you used that one. If this one didn't give you great service, you moved to that one. So when a business has very little in the way of moats, you can't expect it to have very high return on equity or be a wealth winner for you long term. And long before COVID and long before the problems in the Middle East, Hello World had low return on equity. It's still got low return on equity. It does make a profit other than during the COVID period, but it's not gonna be a great business.

headline: Philip Pepe rates Aristocrat Leisure a buy as a defensive, attractively priced market leader with resilient earnings through economic cycles
reasoning: Pepe argues that gaming revenue behaves more like a consumer staple than discretionary spend — it holds up or even increases in economic downturns. Aristocrat is the best-in-class operator, investing heavily in R&D with strong returns on that investment. He sees it as attractively priced by analysts and a good defensive holding in an uncertain macro environment, particularly for investors who can accept the ESG trade-off.
quote: This sector used to be a market darling... If you want to be defensive, like it or not, this is a good company to look at because gaming-related revenue tends to hold up better than not. It is almost a consumer staple rather than consumer discretionary like it or not... They spend a lot of money on R&D and generally got a good return on that investment. Much as I hate to say it, yes, it's a buy. If you can stomach gaming, not so good for the consumer, but it looks pretty cheap. It looks worth owning.

headline: Philip Pepe would sell Brambles, warning of consumer headwinds and rising repair costs with more downside risk ahead
reasoning: Pepe is concerned that Brambles faces sustained headwinds from global cost-of-living pressure, which will weigh on consumer volumes with a lag. He flags that pallet repair costs are rising and he is not convinced the worst is behind the company. He also holds a contrarian view that interest rates globally may not fall — and could even rise in some markets — making the macro backdrop unfavourable. He advises investors not to buy something just because it looks cheap if major headwinds persist.
quote: I'm not of the view that interest rates are coming down anytime soon. I saw some data this morning suggest that certain countries might still put them up. I'm also of the view that the US, their next move is probably up, not down... cost of living is going up globally. That's got to hit consumer volumes with a lag. We're starting to see it in Australia. I think the worst is yet to come in terms of price point, price pressure at the register. And that is a pretty strong headwind for Brambles... I would sit out, I would sell Brambles and buy Hello World on half a multiple.

headline: Philip Pepe sells Cochlear, arguing for the first time implants have proven discretionary with more competition emerging
reasoning: Pepe notes the most alarming revelation from the latest result was that Cochlear implants are to some extent discretionary — people are deferring with hearing aids as an alternative. Competition is increasing with Cenova reportedly targeting the hearing aid space. He is not confident the business model has recovered and advises waiting for at least one more result before reassessing. Given the severity of the first-half miss and downgrade, he warns against chasing a falling stock too aggressively.
quote: The sticker shock with the latest result was I think the first time ever people realised that Cochlear implants are to some extent discretionary. It used to be thought of you need it, you get one. But with price becoming a factor, not just in the Middle East, they have got a Middle East in operations, but with them referrals being down and demand being down or postponed, first time in a long time people realised that maybe this isn't a must-have product... I would sit out and wait for at least the next four-year result and see if more competition comes, see if I can get the audiologist referrals coming back... given the severity of the missed and down grade of the first half result, I would just... I don't chase the falling off too aggressively. Sell.

headline: Philip Pepe rates CSL a sell citing leadership vacuum, VIFOR disaster, China structural headwinds and US immunoglobulin market share losses
reasoning: Pepe argues that when an MD leaves you should simply sell regardless of valuation, and CSL has lost two MDs in short succession with no permanent replacement expected until March. The VIFOR acquisition was a strategic blunder — management failed to anticipate drugs going off patent, a basic error. China price reductions in albumin are structural. US immunoglobulin market share has been lost and the response is to throw money at the problem with little visible R&D pipeline to compensate. The board appears to lack investment acumen. He argues there is no catalyst until a new MD is announced.
quote: Cell, absolute cell... when a managing director leaves a company, just sell, just sell. Don't think valuations, don't think oversold, just sell. This company has lost two... The, forget the name of the company, the VIFOR acquisition, absolute disaster. They did not realise how soon drugs will come... China is structural, they've acknowledged that. Price reductions in albumin, they're here to stay... in milli-globin market in the US, big market, they've lost market share, they're throwing money at the problem... Company is without leadership... My understanding is they won't find someone until March next year. That is a long time for the strategy to be on autopilot, just don't be there, it's a sell.

headline: Philip Pepe would own Monadelphous alongside SRG Global as a core holding in engineering construction sector

headline: Philip Pepe calls Hello World a buy after Friday downgrade, seeing a temporary demand deferral at a cheap 7-8x PE with 7% yield

headline: Philip Pepe rates SRG Global a buy, backed by a five-year bull thesis in engineering construction and exposure to data centres, defence and Olympics

headline: Philip Pepe rates St George Mining a hold for existing shareholders given analyst price targets implying 150-200% upside if correct

headline: Crabbe initiates top pick in Computershare, arguing the share registry giant is positively leveraged to higher rates and a coming wave of mega IPO corporate actions.

Additionally, a wave of mega US IPOs (Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX totalling ~$4 trillion) and increased corporate activity in Australia will drive significant revenue for Computershare's corporate actions and corporate trust businesses. Crabbe notes the stock has only outperformed by about 10% so far and sees material further upside.
quote: I think there's a stock that's really in the crosshairs for us, and that's Computershare. So this is a stock that we haven't traditionally spent a lot of time talking about or thinking about. But Computershare is a share registry business, mostly US-based. They make a lot of money from corporate actions, from corporate trust business, but they also have a large cash float that they look after, and they earn interest margin on that. So when interest rates went up a lot, excuse me, in 2021-2022, Computershare's earnings went up a lot as well. They make something like $700 million a year in interest income on that float. So it's a material number. So where's the view is that rates are not going any lower. In fact, they may drift higher. You want to own stocks that are positively correlated to higher rates. So QBE insurance is one, but Computershare is another.

headline: Crabbe warns Fair Work Commission's 4.75–6% wage rises, combined with negative labour productivity, risk reigniting inflation and pressuring business margins.
reasoning: The Fair Work Commission lifted minimum wages by 6% and award wages by 4.75%, affecting roughly a third of the Australian workforce. Crabbe notes that Australia's GDP-per-hour productivity is negative, meaning businesses must either absorb the cost in margins or pass it through as price increases — both problematic. Bankruptcies are running at record levels, indicating businesses are already under severe stress. Higher wages without productivity gains are inherently inflationary and complicate the RBA's path.
quote: Minimum wages, you know, according to the Fair Work Commission, go up 6% and award wages go up 4.75%. I think it's something like a third of the workforce is either at minimum or award wages. So this is the material impost for businesses. Now, if you're getting productivity, that's fine... The problem is that productivity measured by GDP per hour's work is actually going backwards in Australia. So theoretically, employees are getting less out of each worker and they have to pay them more. It's like that maths doesn't add up. That's got to come from somewhere. Either it's high prices to your customers or you've got to eat it in your margin.

headline: Martin Crabbe sees the SaaS sector bottoming after April lows, with the IGV US software ETF surging 8% as markets reassess the AI-eating-software narrative.

quote: If you look at the ETFs that follows the software names in the US, it popped 8% last night. And the only Aussie stock, that's the IGB. So that's the US Extended Software ETF. And you can see that it's been on a pretty rocky old road since chat. GPT was launched all the way back in not 22. It was up and to the right. And then we've had these kind of concerns about AI eating all the software. And most recently, that bottomed out in about April. headline: Crabbe views the Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX IPO wave as positive for market animal spirits, not a liquidity drain, as these are mostly private-to-public transitions rather than large capital raises.

So it's 2 trillion valuation is mostly money that hedge fund managers and venture capital private equity managers have been putting in along the way... They're going to come onto the market. They're going to be a big part of the index... There's going to be lots of demand. There's not a lot of money being raised. This is more companies that have invested at private equity venture capital stage realizing some of their investments.

headline: Photon assay technology provider sees growing miner adoption but acknowledges need to keep proving value to conservative industry

headline: ASX tech presenter bullish on AI's ability to extract value from years of accumulated data that companies previously didn't know how to use

The really interesting or cool thing for me with AI is being able to have companies and ourselves included plugging all of your data into models where you can have AI working out what to do with that data.

headline: Shore and Partners views Goodman Group as a low-risk, high-quality way to play global AI capex boom despite slight Q3 disappointment
reasoning: Crabb expected Goodman to guide to higher growth (above their 9% guidance) and work-in-progress closer to $17bn vs the $14-15bn reported, so results were slightly below expectations.
